title: Cautions
hookLine: the Kalamas: test a teaching yourself, and trust no one who asks for secrecy or blind obedience (AN 3.65)
last: KALYANAMITTA — THE WHOLE OF THE PATH.

lines: EACH ONE RUNS DOWN THE LAST.
cards: You met the Kalamas back in the story camp. Their town, Kesaputta, was one teachers kept passing through. Each one, the sutta says, explained his own teaching and made it shine, and ran down everyone else's.
Then the next one came and did the same. The Kalamas were left with a plain, tired question: which of these people is telling the truth? When the Buddha came through, they asked him exactly that.
His answer is often quoted, and often quoted wrong.

teach.b: First, the Buddha tells the Kalamas their doubt is reasonable. Then he gives a list, here in paraphrase. Don't go by reports, tradition or hearsay.
Don't go by scripture, logic, inference, what merely seems plausible, or a view you already like. Don't go by how impressive a speaker is, or by the thought, this is our teacher.
Instead, when you know for yourselves that certain things are unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when you act on them, let them go.
When you know things are wholesome, praised by the wise, and lead to well-being, take them up. Then he asks them: does greed lead to benefit or harm? Hatred?
Delusion? And they answer for themselves. Notice what the sutta does not say.
It isn't believe whatever feels right.

teach.h: WATCH THE RESULTS, ASK THE WISE.
teach.b: It points to results you can watch in your own life, and to the judgment of wise people. There's a second caution, and it comes from other texts, not this one.
In a short discourse the Buddha says the sun, the moon and his teaching shine openly; they aren't hidden. And near the end of his life he said he had never held back anything in a closed fist.
Some traditions keep certain practices for students who have prepared, as you saw in the Tibetan weeks.
That's different from secrecy about money, or about how people are treated, or demands for obedience that override your conscience. Those are warning signs anywhere.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite the Kalama Sutta to encourage students to test the teaching in their own experience, and many communities publish codes of conduct and financial information so that students can check a group openly.

o: a list of sins that break a monk's vows
vows of silence taken before a retreat
warnings to test a teaching before trusting it

games.q: match the cautions to where they come from.

s: the Kalama Sutta says believe whatever feels right to you
it points to results you can watch and to the judgment of the wise.
the Buddha told the Kalamas not to go even by scripture
scripture is on the list, alongside tradition, logic and a teacher's reputation.
the warning about secrecy comes from the Kalama Sutta itself
it echoes other texts: the teaching shining openly, and no closed fist.

games.q: you're a Kalama. teacher after teacher says only his way is true. you ask the Buddha whom to believe. what does he tell you?
o: know for yourselves, by results and the judgment of the wise.
games.why: he says their doubt is reasonable, and asks them to see for themselves whether greed, hatred and delusion lead to harm.

practice: Pick one warning sign you'd want to remember in any group, spiritual or not: being told not to ask questions, money nobody explains, being pulled away from friends.
Then sit with the breath and test something right now: does this breath, watched closely, bring agitation or ease? Just look.

wordCard.voice: Cautions. The Buddha told the Kalamas to know for themselves, by results and by the wise, and his teaching shines openly, not in secret.

orig.note: Pali Kālāma: the clan of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha whom to believe (AN 3.65).

carryVoice: Your line: test it yourself. Your doubt, the Buddha said, is reasonable. That's three hundred twenty-one days.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.129 (three things that shine openly)
Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 2.25 (no teacher's closed fist)
